questions_and_answers.question: Carbon capture technologies are considered a key option for reducing CO₂ emissions from power plants and energy-intensive industries. However, large-scale deployment is still limited. I am interested in understanding the major challenges related to capture efficiency, energy penalty, solvent or sorbent degradation, system integration, and overall cost. Insights on the most promising carbon capture methods (post-combustion, pre-combustion, oxy-fuel) and their industrial feasibility would be appreciated.
questions_and_answers.answer: According to BNP Paribas, carbon capture for industrial sectors faces two big obstacles: the technologies still struggle with energy intensity and reliability, and the economics remain difficult because costs are high while revenue streams are uncertain. The latest analyses highlight persistent issues with capture efficiency, integration into existing plants, and the lack of stable business models to justify investment. Technical Challenges 1. High Energy Demand. Most capture methods—especially amine-based post‑combustion capture—require large amounts of heat and electricity to regenerate solvents. This “energy penalty” reduces overall plant efficiency and increases operating costs. 2. Integration With Existing Industrial Processes. Retrofitting cement, steel, chemicals, and refining facilities is complex because flue gas compositions vary widely. questions_and_answers.question: The world’s largest carbon capture and storage (CCS) facility. Designed to remove millions of tons of CO₂ directly from industrial exhaust, this facility is turning one of the planet’s most carbon-intensive regions into a testing ground for industrial-scale climate recovery. The system works at the smokestack level, capturing carbon dioxide, compressing it into liquid form, and injecting it deep into secure geological formations. These underground reservoirs can trap CO₂ safely for thousands of years, preventing it from ever returning to the atmosphere. Alberta’s facility isn’t just big — it’s smart. AI-driven monitoring ensures even microscopic leaks are detected immediately, maintaining airtight safety standards and giving operators real-time control over the massive network. Oil sands operations, cement factories, and power plants are already connected, demonstrating that carbon-intensive industries can coexist with climate mitigation technologies. The potential is massive. If scaled globally, systems like this could offset industrial emissions while renewable energy expands, buying humanity critical time in the fight against climate change. While critics note high upfront costs, the plant’s efficiency, safety, and AI oversight make it a blueprint for the next generation of carbon capture technologies. For Canada, Alberta’s CCS mega-facility is more than a technological feat — it’s a symbol of environmental leadership and a bold vision for industrial transformation, showing the world that even the most polluting regions can be part of the solution. #Canada #CarbonCapture #ClimateAction #CleanTech #SustainableFuture #AlbertaInnovation #GreenIndustry #CarbonNeutral #ClimateSolutions #AIForClimate
questions_and_answers.answer: Carbon capture has a terrible track record of only capturing at best 40% of CO² but using up to 15-25% of the energy produced to do so, meaning more fossil fuels need to be burned to power it. This also makes the end product cost up to a third more. This is why most future projects were abandoned and the money given to renewable energy which has a greater decarbonisation impact per $ spent.

questions_and_answers.question: Australia has begun deploying carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology directly inside its mining operations, turning some of the world’s largest emission sources into experimental climate solutions. In this system, carbon dioxide released during mining is trapped and then pumped deep underground into stable geological layers where it cannot escape back into the atmosphere. For a country heavily reliant on mining, this is a bold step toward balancing industry with climate responsibility. A study published in the International Journal of Greenhouse Gas Control reports that CCS can cut industrial CO₂ emissions by up to 90% when implemented correctly. Meanwhile, research from Australia’s CSIRO emphasizes that coupling CCS with renewable power could accelerate the nation’s net-zero targets by decades. By applying this technology in active mines, Australia is sending a signal to the world: climate change must be fought not only through clean energy but also by transforming the industries most responsible for emissions. This initiative shows how innovation can be woven into even the most polluting sectors. If scaled successfully, it could redefine the future of mining, proving that economic strength and environmental stewardship can evolve side by side.

questions_and_answers.question: How can carbon capture and storage technologies reduce the environmental impact of industrial sectors?
questions_and_answers.answer: It's important to realize that the future of CCS doesn't include a radical reduction in costs due to some new technological invention. Sorting gases from one another is energetically hard to do- innovation can make incremental improvements but cannot "fix" that entirely. It takes a lot of energy, and that energy would either be better used directly OR comes itself from burning fossils without carbon capture. Carbon capture is routine chemical engineering- sequestration is fundamentally more challenging, and will get more expensive as the good reservoirs are filled up.

questions_and_answers.answer: Industrially, I really do not think there are economically viable ones that can carbon capture and geologically store the carbon dioxide nor the carbon capture and chemical fixation of carbon dioxide to create alcohols/lower carbon fuels/chemicals But unless the above technologies are powered by renewable energy sources or even by nuclear power, then the above equation can change. Small scale carbon sequestration/capture experimentation and technological development is still being done in international laboratories. We must also know, as reports say or determine, carbon capture technologies are some inefficient because, as they postulated NOT 100% of the carbon dioxide is actually captured…….but maybe the future holds promise ? Other than the above cons, the largest carbon capturing natural processes are the absorbency of carbon dioxide by photosynthesis of plant life or forests and the oceans retention of carbon dioxide through its own natural process.

questions_and_answers.question: What are the best carbon capture technologies?
questions_and_answers.answer: “Best” depends on the lens: maturity, cost per tonne of CO2 avoided, scaleability, permanence, or suitability to a particular emission source. Below is a structured survey of leading carbon capture technologies (capture + storage/removal), their strengths, limitations, typical use-cases, and maturity so you can match technology to need. 1) Point-source carbon capture (post-combustion) • How it works: CO2 scrubbing from flue gas after combustion using chemical solvents (amines), physical solvents, or solid sorbents. • Strengths: Mature (commercial for decades in industry); retrofit-capable for power plants, cement, steel, refineries; relatively low incremental risk. • Limitations: Energy penalty for solvent regeneration (20–40% of plant output typical for power plants), solvent degradation and corrosion, lower CO2 concentration in flue gas increases cost. • Typical cost & maturity: Capture cost ~ $40–$120+ / tCO2 depending on concentration and plant type; commercially deployed (Sleipner…
